preamble: Click insertion: an inherited Bantu consonant is replaced by a click. This is a sporadic lexical replacement driven by contact with Khoisan languages, not a regular sound change. In Fwe, clicks were acquired through contact with Khwe (Khoe) and Ju varieties (Gunnink et al. 2015, cited in Sands & Gunnink 2019). Sands & Gunnink show that some click words have good Proto-Bantu etymologies in which a plain consonant was replaced. Their example is Fwe -ŋǀùm-ùn-à 'uproot', from Proto-Bantu *-túmʊd-; regular sound change would give Fwe -sùm-ùn-à, and Tonga has -fum-un-a. Wikipedia's Click consonant article gives a second, uncited case of the same kind in a recent loanword: Gciriku cumáte 'tomato', with a dental click, where all neighbouring languages have t. With one etymology and one uncited loanword, certainty is 2.

examples.from: Proto-Bantu *-túmʊd- 'take firewood from fire, tear asunder'
examples.note: Also nasalized. Northern Fwe later lost the click (-ŋùm-ùnà; see click_dental_to_ng). Tonga -fum-un-a 'pull out as grass from thatch' shows the regular reflex.
Gunnink et al. (2015: 231), Table 6; Ila -londa-uka 'to drip'. Voiced click; Gunnink (2022) writes ᵍǀôntà 'drip'. Gunnink et al. (2015: 206) suggest the click imitates the sound of dripping.
Gunnink et al. (2015: 232), Table 6; Tonga tyanga 'pumpkin', in-tanga 'pumpkin seeds'. Gunnink (2022) lists n-tàngà 'pumpkin seeds' and rù-tàngà 'pumpkin stem' with t.

c = dental click [ǀ]. Reported in Wikipedia's Click consonant article, uncited there. This is click insertion in a loanword, not an inherited word. Gunnink et al. (2015: 206), citing Bostoen and Sands (2012: 133), give the same word as Manyo (Gciriku) ǀumáte 'tomato' and call it click insertion, since the Khwe and Ju words for tomato have no click. The sources consulted give only this one example.
